blocks.content: Constitutional bodies derive their authority directly from the Constitution of India, making them independent and resilient to ordinary legislative changes.

rows: Directly mentioned in the Constitution of India
Created by an Act of Parliament or State Legislature
Requires a Constitutional Amendment under Article 368
Can be amended or dissolved by a simple legislative majority
NHRC, SEBI, Central Information Commission (CIC), NGT

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Constitutional bodies derive their powers, duties, and authority directly from specific articles of the Constitution of India.
Any change in the structure, tenure, or powers of a constitutional body requires a constitutional amendment under Article 368.
Major constitutional bodies include the Election Commission (Art. 324), CAG (Art. 148), UPSC (Art. 315-323), and Finance Commission (Art. 280).
The 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendment Acts of 1992 granted constitutional status to Panchayats and Municipalities, adding Part IX and Part IX-A.
Distinguish clearly between Constitutional Bodies (e.g., CAG, UPSC) and Statutory/Non-Constitutional Bodies (e.g., NHRC, NITI Aayog, CVC).
Pay attention to the removal process: Chairpersons of key Constitutional bodies like the CAG and CEC can only be removed in the same manner as a Supreme Court Judge.
Remember that creating or modifying a Constitutional Body requires a Constitutional Amendment Act under Article 368, whereas Statutory Bodies are created by simple legislation.
